pr_body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/49707

This Pull Request has been created because we noticed that `ActiveRecord::Core#inspect` was taking >9s to run for some large objects in production. This is because the parameter filter is be executed for every attribute.

### Detail

This Pull Request introduces configuration for `ActiveRecord::Core#inspect`. By default, `inspect` just returns the object with its id (eg `#<Post id: 1>`. The attributes to include can be configured with `Post.attributes_to_inspect=`. If you want to full output with all the attributes you can call `Post.full_inspect`. 

### Additional information

In my first draft I had a config to disable this, if you just always want to use `full_inspect`. But it seems easy enough just to do `alias_method :inspect, :full_inspect` on the model, or in `ApplicationRecord` if you want to disable it globally. So the config didn't seem worth it to me.

### Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

* [x] This Pull Request is related to one change. Changes that are unrelated should be opened in separate PRs.
* [x] Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: `[Fix #issue-number]`
* [x] Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
* [x] CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.

issue_context.title: `ActiveRecord::Core#inspect` should have an option to not show the attributes in production
issue_context.body:
By mistake, we had a hash containing multiple `ActiveRecord::Base` instance being inspected in production, through `Hash#to_s` call.

This was causing the parameter filter to execute for each attribute, which with the large set of objects we had, end up spending 9s to run.

While this was clearly a mistake, Rails could just help here avoiding the catastrophic results by not listing the attribute by default in production.

If for some reason people want to include their attributes in log message they can use another method that would print the record with attributes (maybe a formatted_inspect). Or they can disable the config per class (or globally)
comments: I am working on implementing a solution for this.

>While this was clearly a mistake, Rails could just help the mistake to not catrastofic results by not listing the attribute by default in production.

Yes. Please!

Hi @rafaelfranca,

Thank you very much for opening this issue. I have linked a PR that I believe will have the solution you are looking for.

Please let me know if there is anything you would like me to fix.

ActiveRecord uses `ActiveSupport::ParameterFilter` to mask attributes defined in `Rails.application.config.filter_parameters` using a deny list.
I'd like to see Rails support masking based on an allow lists instead.

I've an open PR to support parameter filtering based on allow lists: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/45545
It's currently a bit complex, as it supports all the edge cases that `ActiveSupport::ParameterFilter` supports.
An alternative could be making the filtering pluggable, so everyone can write their own filtering class.

Including @matthewd's `ActiveSupport::Inspect` that doesn't render any attributes could work here as well.
https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/45122

review_comments:
I decided to remove this test. `Relation#inspect` calls `inspect` on each of the records. It seems unnatural that virtual columns would be included in `attributes_to_expect` so I didn't want to add that as a test case.

I think we could add a `full_inspect` method to `Relation` if we want to preserve this behaviour.
I think you can rewrite this test in a way that makes sure virtual attributes are inside the loaded record and can be inspected. You could call `full_inspect` in `relation.first`
What if, instead of a separate method, we had an `:all` option? 🤔 e.g. `Post.attributes_to_inspect = :all`. That would make it configurable without needing a separate config.

I think there's a good argument for all of the above.

If a user wants the default behaviour of `.inspect` to be `:all` they should be able to configure it as such without listing all the attributes in the model `attributes_to_inspect = ` as those can change.

A user should also be able to decide to opt into a detailed inspect, without using it as the default.

In this example case we want to make the default to not be harmful, and not accidentally load all attributes deeply for all posts when logging a list:
```ruby
Rails.logger.info("Found these posts: #{ posts.map(&:inspect) }")
```

However, in some examples we do want to really see what's happening, even if it is an expensive operation:
```ruby
Rails.logger.error("This post caused a render error: #{ post.full_inspect }")
```

And finally, we do not want to take away tools from someone who knows what they want. This example model is simple and when we inspect it we really want to see all fields at all times, even if a field gets added or renamed:
```ruby
class Tag < ApplicationRecord
  validates :value, :handle, presence: :true
  attributes_to_inspect = :all
end
```

So just to make sure I understand the suggestion, you want to have `:all` in the `attributes_to_inspect` array. And then in `inspect`, check if `:all` is an element of the array, and if it is, then do a full inspection with all the attributes?

Personally, I dislike using the same array for the list of attributes and for a boolean option like `all`. One issue that comes to mind is what if the model has an attribute called `all`? I guess in `inspect` we can check if the `attributes_to_inspect` array has only one member, and if that one member is `all` then do the full inspection. But now the behaviour is getting convoluted IMO.

What do you guys think about my suggestion that people can just do `alias_method :inspect, :full_inspect` if they always want to do the full inspection by default. Adding it to `ApplicationRecord` would make the upgrade easy.

`:all` would be passed as the option, rather than an array. ie. `Post.attributes_to_inspect = :all`. (`[:all]` would mean "an attribute called all")

@kmcphillips makes a great point about adding support for both `:all` and a `full_inspect` method though -- being able to specify a full inspect as necessary without needing to configure a class attr on the model makes sense for sure.

So maybe:

#### Global config

Use `config.active_record.attributes_to_inspect` to configure the default set of attributes to inspect across all your models. Will default to `[:id]`. Use `config.active_record.attributes_to_inspect = :all` to show all attributes by default.

####  Model-level config

Use `attributes_to_inspect` to configure the default set of attributes to inspect for a given model. e.g the example Kevin provided:
```ruby
class Tag < ApplicationRecord
  validates :value, :handle, presence: :true
  attributes_to_inspect = :all
end
```
#### `#full_inspect`

Use `#full_inspect` to do a full inspection, no matter the global / model config for `attributes_to_inspect`.

IMO, a much more flexible approach would be to make `inspect` accept an optional argument:
```ruby
def inspect(attributes_to_list = [:id])
  if attributes_to_list == :all
    # do full inspection
  else
    # list only the listed attributes
  end
end
```

That way, callers that need the full behaviour will be able to get it by calling `post.inspect(:all)`. In this way the decision can be made per call site, instead of per model. For example, as well as being able to make the  `post.inspect(:all)` call, you could also do a `post.inspect([:id, :title])` for the same `Post` instance, if you wanted to.
Isn’t the problem here that calling Hash#to_s unexpectedly calls inspect on its values instead of to_s?

`Hash#to_s` is just an alias for `inspect` - so it doesn't seem unexpected to me it is calling `inspect` under the hood. Tho yeah, the issue would be fixed if `Hash#to_s` called `to_s` (tho personally I think the outcome would be worse, since `to_s` on AR record doesn't return much useful information imo and the output from inspect is better).
